opus-5.5.text:
I think practical experience matters enormously, maybe more than people outside the field realize. Large-model training isn't something you can fully reason out from papers. There are so many small decisions: how you clean and mix the data, when a loss spike is a real problem versus noise, whether an instability comes from the optimizer, the precision settings, or the data itself. A lot of that judgment only comes from having trained models, watched them fail, and debugged them yourself.

For someone leading a team, experience is valuable in two ways. First, it lets you tell which problems are worth worrying about. When you're spending a huge amount of compute, you can't afford to chase every anomaly, and you also can't afford to miss the one that ruins a run. Experience helps you set those priorities quickly. Second, it builds trust. If you've done the hands-on work, you can talk with researchers and engineers at the level of detail where the real issues are, and they know you understand the trade-offs they're facing.

That said, I don't think experience should turn into dogma. This field changes so fast that something that held true a year ago may not apply at a new scale or with a new architecture. So the most useful kind of experience isn't a fixed set of rules. It's a habit of running careful small-scale experiments, checking your intuitions against data, and being willing to admit when the old intuition is wrong. A good team uses experience to move fast but stays humble about it. You want people who've been burned before, but who are still curious enough to question what they think they know.

r001.rationale: The response values hands-on experience and careful experiments, but does not recommend that team members redo the work together.

fable-5.1.text:
I think practical experience matters enormously, and in a way that's easy to underestimate if you've only read the papers. Training a large model is not primarily a theoretical exercise. It's an engineering and judgment problem where thousands of small decisions compound, and most of those decisions don't have a clean answer you can derive from first principles.

When I think back on the training runs I've been part of, the moments that really tested us were never the ones you plan for. The loss curve suddenly spikes at three in the morning. A data pipeline turns out to have a subtle contamination issue that's been quietly degrading quality for weeks. A hyperparameter that worked beautifully at a smaller scale behaves completely differently when you scale up. In those moments, what saves you is someone on the team who has seen a similar pattern before and can say, "I've seen this shape of problem, let's check this first." That intuition is almost impossible to acquire from reading alone. You earn it by making mistakes, by burning compute on runs that failed, and by sitting with the results long enough to understand why.

So for a leader, I think experience plays two roles. The first is direct: you can make faster, better calls under uncertainty, because you've built a mental library of what tends to go wrong and what tends to work. Scaling laws give you a map, but experience tells you where the map is unreliable.

The second role is more subtle, and I'd argue it's more important. Experience lets you create the conditions for your team to develop their own judgment. If you've been through enough runs, you know which experiments are worth letting a younger researcher own end to end, even if they'll stumble, because that stumble is where the learning happens. You also know when to step in, because some mistakes are too expensive to allow. Finding that balance is itself a skill you only get through having been on both sides.

I'd add one caveat, though. Experience can become a liability if you treat it as doctrine. This field moves so fast that lessons from two years ago can be actively misleading today. What worked for a dense model may not transfer to a mixture-of-experts architecture. Data recipes that were optimal at one scale can be wrong at the next. So the kind of experience I value most is not "I know the answer," but "I know how to quickly find out whether my prior still holds." The best people I've worked with hold their hard-won intuitions firmly enough to act on them, and loosely enough to abandon them when the evidence says so.

In the end, I'd say practical experience is the thing that turns a group of smart people into a team that can actually ship a frontier model. The ideas are increasingly shared across the industry. The difference comes down to execution, and execution is where experience lives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning through experiments and when a leader should step in, but it does not recommend having team members redo the work together or contrast that with prescribing steps for everyone to follow.

astra-6.text:
I think practical experience helps you distinguish between knowing how training is supposed to work and knowing what to do when it doesn’t. You can understand the methods, but when a run becomes unstable or an evaluation stops improving, you still have to decide what to investigate first and whether there’s enough evidence to change course.

For someone guiding a team, that experience should translate into a clearer process: make the hypothesis explicit, choose an experiment that can test it, and record what you learn. Otherwise, you can spend a lot of compute without reducing uncertainty.

But experience shouldn’t become authority that nobody can question. A past solution is a useful starting point, not a guarantee. The goal is to help the team build its own judgment, so people can explain both what they’re doing and why the evidence supports it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends making hypotheses explicit, choosing experiments, and recording lessons, but it does not say team members should redo the work together. It also does not contrast that recommendation with prescribing steps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think practical experience helps you develop judgment about where to look when something goes wrong. In large-model training, a disappointing result can come from the data, the optimization, the infrastructure, or the way you evaluate the model. The challenge is deciding which possibility to investigate first.

For someone leading a team, that experience is valuable only if you can turn it into a shared way of working. You need to explain why you’re making a decision, keep good records of experiments, and help people connect the results to their assumptions. Otherwise, everyone depends on one person’s intuition.

At the same time, experience shouldn’t become a fixed recipe. What worked in one training run may fail at a different scale. I would use experience to choose the next experiment, then let the evidence decide whether that judgment was right.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends shared decision-making, experiment records, and using evidence to guide experiments, but does not recommend having team members redo the work together.
